$comment: Sources. Each claim, phrase and asset points to these IDs. type: official | site | press | secondary | reference checked: date the page was read for this project.

sources.title: Vietnamese etiquette for travellers — vietnam.travel
sources.org: Vietnam National Authority of Tourism (official site)
sources.used: Forms of address, “bạn ơi”, greeting the eldest first, shared meals, passing with both hands or the right hand, hosts serving guests, declining food, toasting with “dô”, shoes and hats at temples, asking before photos.
sources.limits: General advice for travellers, no publication date shown. Not specific to Hanoi or to any one household.

sources.short: Văn Miếu – Quốc Tử Giám visitor rules
sources.title: Visitor information & rules (Nội quy) — vanmieu.gov.vn
sources.org: Văn Miếu – Quốc Tử Giám Centre for Cultural and Scientific Activities
sources.used: Respectful dress in worship areas, keeping quiet, not touching or writing on stelae and artefacts, no smoking, ban on superstitious practices, opening hours.
sources.limits: In Vietnamese. Does not mention photography or incense; rules can change, so check on the day.

sources.title: Stone stele records of royal examinations of the Lê and Mạc dynasties
sources.org: UNESCO Memory of the World Committee for Asia and the Pacific (MOWCAP)
sources.used: 82 surviving stelae of 85, exams 1442–1779, erected 1484–1780, inscribed 2010 (regional) and 2011 (international), they record the names of doctoral laureates.
sources.limits: Does not explain the meaning of the turtle bases.

sources.title: Common Vietnamese names and forms of address
sources.used: anh / chị / em, cô / chú / bác; a bare first name without a title is often felt to be impolite.
sources.limits: Travel-marketing guide, not a linguistic source. Treated as “being verified”.

sources.title: Temple etiquette keeps visitors in sacred harmony
sources.used: Background on covering shoulders and knees and observing quietly at temples.
sources.limits: Newspaper feature about temples in general, not about Văn Miếu.

sources.title: Vietnamese chopstick etiquette: a traveler’s guide
sources.used: Chopsticks standing upright in rice recall incense at funerals.
sources.limits: Third-party blog. Not confirmed by an official or academic source yet.

sources.title: Understanding Success Criterion 2.5.7: Dragging Movements
sources.used: Every pointer interaction has a single-click alternative and keyboard support.
sources.limits: Design reference only; this prototype does not claim WCAG conformance.

sources.title: Understanding Success Criterion 2.3.3: Animation from Interactions
sources.used: Reduce-motion and text-first settings.
sources.limits: AAA criterion, used as guidance only.

sources.short: W3C — Making Audio and Video Media Accessible
sources.title: Making Audio and Video Media Accessible
sources.used: Every audio phrase has a transcript and meaning.
sources.limits: Guidance only.

sources.short: Law on Road Traffic Order and Safety 2024, Art. 30
sources.title: Luật Trật tự, an toàn giao thông đường bộ (No. 36/2024/QH15), Điều 30 — Người đi bộ
sources.org: National Assembly of Vietnam (law text read on the hethongphapluat.com legal database)
sources.used: Art. 30(1)(b): pedestrians may cross only where there are traffic lights, a marked crossing, or a pedestrian bridge or tunnel, and must follow signals; where there are none, they must watch oncoming vehicles, cross only when it is safe and give a hand signal while crossing. In force since 1 January 2025.
sources.limits: In Vietnamese. Read on a legal database, not the Official Gazette. The law does not say how far away a crossing has to be before the “no crossing” rule applies.

sources.title: Người đi bộ không ra tín hiệu bằng tay khi sang đường cũng có thể bị phạt
sources.org: Cổng Thông tin điện tử tỉnh Hà Tĩnh (republishing Đời sống & Pháp luật)
sources.used: Crossing without the required hand signal can be fined 150,000–250,000 đồng under Decree 168/2024 (Art. 10).
sources.limits: In Vietnamese. A news article on a government portal (15 January 2025), not the decree itself.

sources.title: Vietnam travel advice: safety and security — GOV.UK
sources.used: Compliance with road laws is poor; be aware of motorcycles approaching as you walk; bag-snatching by thieves on motorcycles is common, so hold bags in front of you or on the side away from the traffic.
sources.limits: Written for British travellers to all of Vietnam. Safety advice, not etiquette. No update date shown on the page we read.

sources.title: Vietnam Survival Guide: Road Crossing 101
sources.org: Vietcetera (Vietnamese media company), by Quynh Anh, 22 November 2024
sources.used: Walk at a consistent, even pace in a straight line so your next move is predictable; rushing or zigzagging can confuse drivers; if unsure, position yourself behind local pedestrians and move when they do.
sources.limits: Lifestyle guide, not official road-safety advice. Treated as “being verified” until an official source says the same.

sources.title: A beginner’s guide to Vietnamese street food — vietnam.travel
sources.org: Vietnam National Authority of Tourism (official site)
sources.used: Ordering at the front, pointing and “một suất”, sharing tables at busy times, free herbs with noodle dishes, trà đá, wiping chopsticks, “eat first, pay later”.
sources.limits: General advice for the whole country, no publication date shown. Not specific to Hà Nội or to one stall.

sources.title: Vietnam Survival Guide: Bargaining 101
sources.used: Bargaining is common in local markets; politeness and rapport; “Không, cảm ơn” and walking away.
sources.limits: A lifestyle article (5 December 2024), not an official source. Its advice to open at half the quoted price is not used here.

sources.title: Book tells bygone memories of Hà Nội’s iconic Đồng Xuân Market
sources.used: Built in 1889 during the French colonial period to replace the Kẻ Chợ markets.
sources.limits: A news article about a book (9 October 2025); it does not describe the market’s later rebuilding.

sources.title: Five most popular markets in Hanoi
sources.org: Hanoi Times (Hà Nội People’s Committee’s English-language outlet)
sources.used: Ground-floor wet market; upper levels selling fabric, clothing and other goods, often wholesale.
sources.limits: No publication date shown; layout may have changed.

sources.title: Ngoc Son Temple
sources.used: Who the temple honours, its 1841 building and 1865 repair under Nguyễn Văn Siêu; the stone Pen Tower with its brush-shaped top and “Tả Thanh Thiên” inscription; the Ink Slab on three frogs; the red Thê Húc (“Sunbeam”) bridge.
sources.limits: A short official page last updated 16 March 2011; it gives no height for the tower.

sources.title: Hoan Kiem Lake
sources.org: Vietnam National Authority of Tourism (SEA Games 31 visitor site)
sources.used: The meaning of the name and the legend of Lê Lợi returning the sword to the Golden Turtle God in 1428.
sources.limits: A visitor page made for the 2022 SEA Games; it tells the legend as a legend, not as history.

sources.title: Văn Miếu – Quốc Tử Giám, trường đại học cổ nhất Việt Nam
sources.used: Văn Miếu built in 1070 under Lý Thánh Tông; Quốc Tử Giám set up beside it in 1076 under Lý Nhân Tông; Khuê Văn Các built in 1805; Thiên Quang Tỉnh, the square pond.
sources.limits: A newspaper feature from 21 July 2009, in Vietnamese.

sources.title: Vietnamese culture: Greetings
sources.org: Cultural Atlas (cultural reference site, first published by SBS Australia), by Nina Evason
sources.used: People are usually addressed by their given name together with an honorific, normally a family (kinship) term chosen by age, gender and status.
sources.limits: A general reference for Vietnamese culture (2024 edition), not specific to Hà Nội; it does not say outright that a bare first name is rude.

sources.title: Vietnamese culture: Etiquette — The Cultural Atlas
sources.org: The Cultural Atlas (Mosaica), Cultural Atlas Editors
sources.used: Passing and receiving with both hands; givers playing down a gift and hosts playing down a meal; complimenting the food; gifts thought to be bad omens; not standing chopsticks upright in rice; thanking sincerely rather than by reflex.
sources.limits: A general guide (2016) for Vietnam as a whole; it notes regional differences in places.

sources.title: Knowing table manners, knowing social values of a country
sources.org: VOV5, the foreign-language service of Voice of Vietnam (national broadcaster)
sources.used: A Vietnamese tour guide: sticking chopsticks straight into the bowl is a taboo because it reminds people of a funeral, where incense is stuck into rice for the dead.
sources.limits: A feature quoting a tour guide and foreign residents; no date shown on the page.

sources.title: What is it about crossing the streets in Vietnam?
sources.org: Tuổi Trẻ News (English edition of a national daily), by contributor Ray Kuschert
sources.used: Walk slowly, raise your arm and look at riders; don’t step backwards when you panic — stand still and let motorbikes go around you.
sources.limits: A personal column by a long-term resident (17 January 2025), not official road-safety advice.

sources.title: Rules for crossing the street in Vietnam’s major cities
sources.org: Tuổi Trẻ News (English edition of a national daily), by Terry F. Buss
sources.used: Wait until a group of local people is about to cross, and cross with them.
sources.limits: A light-hearted expat column (25 July 2014), not official advice.

sources.title: A guide to shopping in VN
sources.org: VietNamNet Global (national news site), by David Mann
sources.used: Bargaining is for street vendors and places without printed price tags; keep it light and friendly, a smile helps; you can walk away.
sources.limits: An expat column from 28 November 2013; prices and habits may have changed.

sources.title: Vietnamese culture: Religion — Cultural Atlas
sources.used: Ancestral altars, when ancestors are honoured (death anniversaries, the 1st and 15th of the lunar month, Tết), filial piety, village tutelary spirits, Mother Goddess worship being more common in the north.
sources.limits: An educational overview written for an Australian audience (2025). Not specific to Hà Nội or to any one family.

sources.title: Bia tiến sĩ tại Văn Miếu – Quốc Tử Giám là Di sản tư liệu thế giới — Tuổi Trẻ
sources.used: The first doctoral stele was erected in 1484 for the 1442 examination and the last in 1780; the line “Hiền tài là nguyên khí quốc gia” on the first stele.
sources.limits: News report in Vietnamese (2010). The English translation of the quotation is ours.

sources.title: Hỏi các nhà sử học — Nhân Dân
sources.used: The 1442 examination as the first whose laureates were carved on a stele; ten stelae erected together in 1484; the source of the “hiền tài” quotation.
sources.limits: A short reader Q&A in Vietnamese. Its count of laureates (1,306) differs slightly from other sources, so we do not quote a number.

sources.title: Lunar New Year — vietnam.travel
sources.org: Vietnam National Authority of Tourism (official site)
sources.used: How families prepare for Tết (cooking, cleaning, paying respects to ancestors), flowering trees, lucky money called “mừng tuổi” in the north and “lì xì” in the south.
sources.limits: An events listing for Tết 2023; general and brief.

sources.title: “Xông đất” – a cherished Lunar New Year tradition — Vietnam Pictorial (VNA)
sources.used: The first visitor of the year (xông đất) and the belief that this person bears on a household’s fortune.
sources.limits: Feature article (2020); describes the custom in general terms.

sources.title: Unique traditional Tet customs of Vietnam — VietNamNet
sources.used: Families visiting ancestors’ graves in the last week of the lunar year to invite them home for Tết; visiting and lucky money in the first days.
sources.limits: General feature; customs vary by family and region.

sources.title: Votive paper burnt in Hanoi’s Old Quarter — DTiNews
sources.used: Votive paper burnt on Old Quarter streets on the 15th day of the seventh lunar month, and concern about smoke, fire risk and waste.
sources.limits: Short photo report (2022).

sources.title: Hang Ma street: a glittering space of buoyant businesses — Hanoi Times
sources.used: Hàng Mã as an Old Quarter street of paper offerings and paper ornaments, with tube houses typical of the quarter.
sources.limits: Feature article; no date shown in the text we read.

sources.title: Hang Ma Street — vietnamtourism.com
sources.used: That “mã” refers to paper goods made for offerings, and that families burn paper money for their ancestors on the 1st and 15th of the lunar month.
sources.limits: A private travel website, not the national tourism authority despite its name. Treated as “being verified”.

sources.title: Temple etiquette in Vietnam — vietnamtourism.com
sources.used: The difference between chùa (Buddhist pagoda), đền (temple to a hero, king or deity) and đình (village communal house for guardian spirits).
sources.limits: A private travel website. The distinction is widely repeated, but real sites often combine all three. Treated as “being verified”.

sources.title: Decision 34 COM 8B.22: Central Sector of the Imperial Citadel of Thang Long – Hanoi
sources.used: The inscription of the Central Sector of the Imperial Citadel of Thăng Long – Hà Nội on the World Heritage List in 2010.
sources.limits: An official decision text; it does not describe what visitors see.

sources.title: Imperial Citadel of Thang Long — hoangthanhthanglong.vn
sources.org: Thang Long – Hanoi Heritage Conservation Centre (official site)
sources.used: Thăng Long – Hà Nội’s thousand years counted from King Lý Thái Tổ’s decision to move the capital here in 1010.
sources.limits: The site’s own listing page; we read the summaries, not every article.

sources.title: Central Sector of the Imperial Citadel of Thang Long – Ha Noi — Vietnam heritage pages
sources.org: Vietnam National Authority of Tourism (official site)
sources.used: Đoan Môn as the main gate of the Forbidden City, facing south; the site covering about 18 hectares with the archaeological area at 18 Hoàng Diệu.
sources.limits: General heritage summary, no publication date shown.

sources.title: Practices related to the Viet beliefs in the Mother Goddesses of Three Realms
sources.used: The Mother Goddesses of the realms of heaven, water, and mountains and forests; Liễu Hạnh as Mother of the World; inscription in 2016.
sources.limits: UNESCO’s summary of Vietnam’s nomination file.

sources.title: Practices related to the Việt beliefs in the Mother Goddesses of Three Realms receive inscription — UN Viet Nam press release
sources.used: Daily worship, ceremonies and the lên đồng (mediumship) ritual; that the practice is believed to have developed since the 16th century.
sources.limits: Press release, 5 December 2016.

sources.title: Practices related to the Viet Beliefs in the Mother Goddesses of Three Realms — Vietnam heritage pages
sources.org: Vietnam National Authority of Tourism (official site)
sources.used: That the belief is open to everyone regardless of age, occupation or religion, and is practised mainly in the north and north-central regions.
sources.limits: General heritage summary.

sources.title: Explore the Old Quarter your way — vietnam.travel
sources.org: Vietnam National Authority of Tourism (official site)
sources.used: The 36 guild streets named after trades that supplied the court at the Thăng Long citadel; few streets still sell their goods; Hàng Bạc, Hàng Mã, Hàng Gai and Lãn Ông today; tube houses; Ô Quan Chưởng as the last gate, built 1749 and rebuilt 1817; Chinese merchant families; the weekend walking streets.
sources.limits: A visitor guide with no date or references. It gives the “pink dye” name to Hàng Gai, which belongs to Hàng Đào, so we do not use that line.

sources.title: Sidewalk iced tea, an indispensable part of Hanoians’ life — Hanoi Times
sources.used: How a trà đá stall is set up, what else it sells, when people drink it and who sits there.
sources.limits: Feature article; no publication date shown in the text we read.

sources.title: Hanoi curbs kerb culture with clampdown on pavement vendors — AFP, published by The Star
sources.org: Agence France-Presse (republished by The Star, Malaysia)
sources.used: Pavements long tolerated as space for stalls, parking and drinkers on low stools; nearly 2,000 surveillance cameras; fines of up to 6 million đồng for businesses and 250,000 đồng for vendors; more than 3,000 fines since December 2025 according to state media; a flower seller moved to a vacant lot whose takings halved; earlier campaigns short-lived.
sources.limits: A wire report of June 2026. Its vendor fine is a tenth of the figure VnExpress gives; it names no streets.

sources.title: Streets around Hoan Kiem Lake officially become pedestrianized on weekends — Hanoi Times
sources.used: The weekend walking space around Hoàn Kiếm Lake: Friday to Sunday evenings, its hours and cultural events.
sources.limits: Report from December 2019. Hours and the streets included have changed over the years; check locally.

sources.title: Hanoi’s pho declared national intangible heritage — Hanoi Times
sources.used: Hà Nội phở listed as national intangible cultural heritage in August 2024; phở as an early-1900s street snack; beef and chicken versions; what comes with a bowl; the number of phở shops.
sources.limits: News report (2024). It does not name the issuing authority or decision number.

sources.title: Local noodle soup designated as national intangible cultural heritage — The Investor
sources.used: Phở Nam Định was also recognised as national intangible cultural heritage by the Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism in 2024.
sources.limits: News report, 13 August 2024.

sources.title: Bún chả: a tasty feast of colours and flavours — Viet Nam News
sources.used: What bún chả is made of, its dipping sauce and herbs, how it is eaten, when Hanoians eat it, and what writer Thạch Lam said about it.
sources.limits: Feature article, 1 November 2016.

sources.title: Wake up and smell the egg coffee — VietNamNet
sources.used: The origin of egg coffee with Nguyễn Văn Giang in the 1940s, Café Giảng (1946), how it is made and served.
sources.limits: Feature article, June 2020. The origin story comes from the family that runs the café.

sources.title: Decision 6398/QĐ-UBND (24 October 2013): planning and architecture regulation for the Hà Nội Old Quarter
sources.used: The Old Quarter’s official extent (about 82 ha, 10 wards, 79 streets) and boundary streets; the 2004 national heritage listing it cites; the rules to keep tube houses, inner courtyards, pre-1954 buildings and tiled roofs, and to allow no large shopping centres.
sources.limits: A legal text, read on a third-party legal database whose later articles were only partly visible. Ward names changed after the 2025 reorganisation of Hà Nội’s wards.

sources.title: Ô Quan Chưởng – cửa ô duy nhất còn lại của Hà Nội — Nhân Dân
sources.used: Ô Quan Chưởng built in 1749 as Đông Hà Môn; 21 gates in early-nineteenth-century records and 16 in 1831; the name linked to a Chưởng cơ who fought the French in 1873; its two storeys, three arches and old wooden doors; Hàng Chiếu, the mat street, beside it.
sources.limits: A weekend feature in Vietnamese (October 2024); it does not date the later repairs.

sources.title: Hà Nội từng có 21 cửa ô — VnExpress
sources.used: The wall rebuilt under Lord Trịnh Doanh in 1749; old geographies counting 21 gates, maps showing 15 or 16; the 1881 stele of Governor Hoàng Diệu on the gate; André Masson’s account that the gate was saved from demolition in 1906 by the École française d’Extrême-Orient.
sources.limits: A feature in Vietnamese (December 2016) by a writer on Hà Nội, citing old books and maps rather than giving references.

sources.title: Tên gọi Ô Quan Chưởng có ý nghĩa gì? — VTC News
sources.used: Three explanations of the gate’s name; repairs in 1785 and rebuilding in 1804; the characters Đông Hà Môn above the arch; the local story of residents refusing to sign for its demolition; its listing as a historical and cultural relic in 1994.
sources.limits: A short explainer in Vietnamese (August 2026). Its rebuilding dates differ from the tourism authority’s 1817.

sources.title: Hàng Bạc Street — Viet Nam Government Portal, Hà Nội Capital
sources.org: Viet Nam Government Portal (thanglong.chinhphu.vn), by Carol Howland
sources.used: Hàng Bạc as a centre of gold, silver and money exchange for centuries; the silver-ingot workshop set up at No. 58 by Lưu Xuân Tín under Lê Thánh Tông; the two communal houses of the silversmiths.
sources.limits: A feature written in 2010 for the government’s English-language Hà Nội pages; some Vietnamese names are misspelt in it.

sources.title: Giữ lửa nghề truyền thống ở làng chế tác vàng bạc 500 năm tuổi ở Hải Dương — VietnamPlus
sources.used: Châu Khê, the silversmith village whose people founded Hàng Bạc; Lưu Xuân Tín casting silver ingots for the capital under Lê Thánh Tông (1460–1497); the ingot work later moving to Huế while the craftsmen stayed as jewellers; craftsmen from Định Công and Đồng Xâm joining them.
sources.limits: A news feature (January 2024) that retells the village’s history as recorded tradition, without references.

sources.title: Đình Kim Ngân đón Bằng Di tích quốc gia — Nhân Dân
sources.used: Kim Ngân communal house on Hàng Bạc, built by people from Châu Khê, honouring the founder of the hundred crafts; its ranking as a national relic in October 2012.
sources.limits: A short news report (March 2013).

sources.title: Không gian kể chuyện đình Kim Ngân: Đánh thức ký ức phường nghề phố cổ Hà Nội — VOV
sources.used: The storytelling exhibition at Kim Ngân communal house in 2025, with demonstrations of silver-leaf work and repoussé, run by the Hoàn Kiếm Lake and Old Quarter Management Board.
sources.limits: News of a temporary exhibition (November–December 2025).

sources.title: Quận Hoàn Kiếm đón bằng công nhận Di tích quốc gia đặc biệt đền Bạch Mã — Nhân Dân
sources.used: Bạch Mã temple as the eastern of the four guardian temples of Thăng Long, worshipping the god Long Đỗ; the white-horse legend, told as legend; its festival on the 12th and 13th of the second lunar month; the 2022 special national relic ranking (Decision 93/QĐ-TTg).
sources.limits: A report of the ranking ceremony (June 2022).

sources.title: Thăm đền Bạch Mã: Theo dấu ngựa trắng dựng thành Thăng Long — Đại biểu Nhân dân
sources.org: Đại biểu Nhân dân (newspaper of the National Assembly)
sources.used: The white-horse legend as recorded in the fourteenth-century Việt điện u linh tập, according to Prof. Đinh Khắc Thuân; the temple’s nineteenth-century Nguyễn architecture; its 17 steles and 21 royal decrees; its 1986 national listing.
sources.limits: A feature (February 2026) quoting historians; the founding date it gives rests on legend.

sources.title: History through Hà Nội’s architecture — Việt Nam News
sources.used: Đồng Xuân market built by the French in 1889, with a double iron roof for ventilation; the 1886 municipal council meant to make Hà Nội a “European city”; the city of citadel, Old Quarter and countryside before colonial rule; tube houses kept beside French villas.
sources.limits: A feature (May 2018) quoting architects, without references.

sources.title: Rue des Changeurs, Hanoi (André Salles, 1896) — Wikimedia Commons
sources.org: Wikimedia Commons (scan of a photograph by André Salles)
sources.used: That the French called Hàng Bạc “rue des Changeurs” (money changers’ street) in the 1890s, as the photograph’s title records.
sources.limits: An archive photograph and its title, not a history.

sources.title: hàng — Wiktionary
sources.used: The meaning of “hàng”: goods, wares, merchandise (also a row or line).
sources.limits: A community dictionary, used only for the everyday meaning of the word.

sources.title: Hanoi street vendors move off sidewalks as encroachment crackdown tightens — VnExpress International
sources.used: Plan 332 and its three stages; camera fines issued remotely; a vendor fine of 2.5 million đồng with equipment seized; about 1,100 streets with pavements and a 2025 survey finding over 90% of 120 streets encroached; where a bún riêu stall, an iced-tea stand and a xôi stall moved; an economist’s call for designated vending zones.
sources.limits: A news feature of May 2026. Its vendor fine differs from AFP’s.

sources.title: Hà Nội to ramp up urban order campaign starting December 13 — Việt Nam News
sources.used: The campaign’s start at 7 a.m. on 13 December 2025, its three phases to the end of March 2026, the aim of ending informal street markets and changing “outdated habits”.
sources.limits: A report of the plan before it began (December 2025).

sources.title: Hà Nội: Camera AI vào cuộc “phạt nguội”, trật tự đô thị từng bước đi vào nề nếp — Đại biểu Nhân dân
sources.org: Đại biểu Nhân dân (newspaper of the National Assembly), by Nhật Trường
sources.used: Plan 332/KH-UBND of 10 December 2025; fines issued afterwards from camera images; about 848 cases in the first week, 269 found by cameras including AI cameras; pilot camera centres at ward police in Ô Chợ Dừa and Tây Hồ.
sources.limits: A report in Vietnamese (January 2026) based on police figures.

sources.title: Vietnam’s biggest cities push to reclaim sidewalks, drawing praise, nostalgia, and skepticism — Tuổi Trẻ News
sources.org: Tuổi Trẻ News, by Bao Anh
sources.used: The pilot in the central wards of Hoàn Kiếm, Cửa Nam and Ba Đình; vendors asked to bring goods indoors; residents who found it strange at first but welcomed the walking space.
sources.limits: A feature of January 2026 that also covers Hồ Chí Minh City.

sources.title: Ha Noi: Local pavements cleared in urban order crackdown — Government News
sources.org: Viet Nam Government Portal (en.baochinhphu.vn), by Kim Loan
sources.used: Streets cleared (Hàng Mã, Hàng Ngang, Hàng Đào, Phùng Hưng, Tràng Tiền, Đinh Tiên Hoàng and around Hoàn Kiếm Lake); day and evening inspections; the government’s view that central pavements are noticeably less congested.
sources.limits: The government’s own account (May 2026); its results are not independently measured.

sources.title: Encroachment on roadways and pavements in Hà Nội to be fined up to $220 — Việt Nam News
sources.used: A draft city resolution under the 2026 Law on the Capital: 4–6 million đồng for using roads or pavements for markets, food service or displays, 1.2–2 million for pavement parking, double for organisations, from next year if approved.
sources.limits: Reports a draft (May 2026). We did not confirm whether it has been passed.

sources.title: Hanoi Rolls Out $1.7 Sidewalk Leasing. But Is It Economical? — Vietcetera
sources.used: A draft pilot to lease pavement for trade at 20,000–45,000 đồng per square metre a month, on streets at least 3 m wide outside heritage zones, keeping 1.5 m clear and with the consent of half the households.
sources.limits: Reports a draft (May 2026) with no adoption date.

sources.title: Locals retake Hanoi’s sidewalks as cleanup campaign dies down — VnExpress International
sources.org: VnExpress International, by Pham Du and Quang Chien
sources.used: The 2017 campaign: begun in late February, a three-step plan from 10 March, and by May ramps, parked motorbikes and tea sellers back on the pavements.
sources.limits: A news report of May 2017.

sources.title: Hanoi sidewalk tea’s spirit of the streets — VnExpress International
sources.used: A glass once cost as little as 500 đồng; ice arriving under French rule from a factory on Trần Nhật Duật Street, and Hanoians icing drinks by the early 1920s; stalls busy from morning until late; customers from all walks of life; the tea seller as the street’s source of news.
sources.limits: A travel feature (June 2024) without references for its history.

sources.title: Trà Đá: Vietnam’s Most Common Drink Tells A Collective Memory — Vietcetera
sources.used: The stall as a kettle, a thermos and rows of low stools; the view that iced tea became a northern habit after 1975 and spread through Hà Nội in the 1990s.
sources.limits: A magazine essay; its year of publication is not shown on the page. Its history differs from VnExpress’s.

sources.title: Sidewalk iced tea culture in Hanoi — VietNamNet
sources.org: VietNamNet (credited to Việt Nam News), by Le Ha
sources.used: What a stall holds (thermos, teapot, jar of sweets, tobacco pipe, plastic chairs); regulars who meet every morning; a seller at Ô Quan Chưởng for decades; tea shops as places to chat and share news.
sources.limits: A feature of July 2016.

sources.title: Contesting Street Spaces in a Socialist City: Itinerant Vending-Scapes and the Everyday Politics of Mobility in Hanoi, Vietnam — Annals of the American Association of Geographers 106(2): 340–349
sources.org: Annals of the American Association of Geographers (peer-reviewed), N. Eidse, S. Turner and N. Oswin
sources.used: Eight months of fieldwork with 305 Hà Nội vendors, most of them women and most itinerant migrants from farming households; carrying-pole loads of up to 45 kg; the 1984 rule reserving pavements for walking and the 1991 campaign; moving on as a way to stay in the city.
sources.limits: Fieldwork from the early 2010s; it describes vendors, not customers.

sources.title: Shared Streets: Choreographed Disorder in the Late Socialist City — Politics and Governance 11(2): 305–314
sources.org: Politics and Governance (peer-reviewed, open access), S. Kurfürst
sources.used: Street trade, mostly by women, growing after Đổi Mới; Decision 02/2008 banning trade on 62 streets and at 48 historic sites from 1 July 2008; police taking stools and tables; vendors with shoulder poles and bicycles slipping into alleys; campaigns fading after a few months.
sources.limits: Based on fieldwork from 2007 to 2018. Another study counts 63 streets under the 2008 ban.

sources.title: Ngọc Sơn Temple and Hoàn Kiếm Lake — Viet Nam Government Portal, Hà Nội Capital
sources.used: The lake’s earlier name Lục Thủy (Green Water) and its renaming in the fifteenth century after the legend of Lê Lợi and the tortoise; the history of Ngọc Sơn Temple from a temple to Guan Yu to the 1841 Association of Good Deeds and its rebuilding in 1859–1862; Trần Hưng Đạo and Văn Xương; the Pen Tower; a turtle 2.1 m long found in 1967.
sources.limits: A government feature of July 2010 with no author; it tells the sword story as legend.

sources.title: Ngoc Son Temple: A historic spiritual haven in Hanoi — VnExpress International
sources.used: The temple on Jade Island honouring Trần Hưng Đạo and Văn Xương; the scholar Nguyễn Văn Siêu’s works of 1865 and the curved red Thê Húc bridge; the Pen Tower and Ink Slab; two preserved turtles on display; opening hours and the 50,000 đồng ticket.
sources.limits: A travel feature of January 2025; hours and prices may change. Its date for Nguyễn Văn Siêu’s work differs from the government page.

sources.title: Turtle tower: The architectural landmark of Hoan Kiem lake — VietNamNet
sources.used: The tower built in 1884–1886 by Nguyễn Ngọc Kim, said to be a pretext to bury his parents on the islet; the earlier pavilion of Lê Thánh Tông and the Trịnh lords’ temple on the mound; brick storeys with Gothic arches under a Vietnamese roof.
sources.limits: A feature of August 2018. Other accounts give the builder’s name, the date and the number of storeys differently.

sources.title: Vietnam’s giant turtle in Hoan Kiem Lake dies — Tuổi Trẻ News
sources.used: The turtle found dead on the afternoon of 19 January 2016; its 2011 measurements of 185 cm and 169 kg; old age and cold weather given as causes; its body taken to Ngọc Sơn Temple and then the Vietnam National Museum of Nature.
sources.limits: A news report of January 2016.

sources.title: Hanoi Perspectives: Morning Exercise by the Lake — Vietcetera
sources.used: Group exercise from 6 a.m., with some people arriving around 5 to meet friends; dancing groups behind an instructor, older women at tai chi, older men jogging, younger men doing push-ups.
sources.limits: A photo feature (about 2016) covering both Hoàn Kiếm and West Lake.

sources.title: Getting the kinks out — Việt Nam News
sources.org: Việt Nam News, by Richard Henderson
sources.used: The walk around the lake as a loop of about 1.5 km; people walking, jogging and giving each other back massages in the morning.
sources.limits: A column of October 2012.

sources.title: Hà Nội: Khai trương tuyến phố đi bộ quanh hồ Hoàn Kiếm — VietnamPlus
sources.used: The walking space opened on the evening of 1 September 2016, from 7 p.m. on Friday to midnight on Sunday, on about 15 streets including Đinh Tiên Hoàng, Hàng Khay, Tràng Tiền and Lê Thái Tổ, closed to all vehicles.
sources.limits: A report of the opening night (September 2016). Another report counts 14 streets.

sources.title: Hoan Kiem walking street: where Hanoi comes alive during weekends — VnExpress International
sources.used: Hours of 7 p.m. Friday to midnight Sunday; 25,000–35,000 visitors a weekend and up to 50,000 at Tết.
sources.limits: A feature of August 2023. It calls September 2016 the official opening after a pilot, while other reports call it the start of the pilot.

sources.title: Hà Nội: Chính thức thí điểm vùng phát thải thấp trong Vành đai 1 từ ngày 1/7 — Báo Xây dựng
sources.org: Báo Xây dựng (newspaper of the Ministry of Construction), by Mai Thu
sources.used: The city council’s approval of a low-emission pilot zone on 15 June 2026: first phase limited to part of Hoàn Kiếm ward, with vehicles kept out from 7 p.m. to midnight on Friday to Sunday around the lake and the night market; the city not yet banning petrol motorbikes outright, with the wider limits moved to 2028.
sources.limits: A report of the approval (June 2026), in Vietnamese.

sources.title: Hanoi begins vehicle ban in Hoan Kiem low-emission zone — DTiNews
sources.used: The zone starting on the evening of 3 July 2026, with motorbikes and cars barred from 12 streets between 7 p.m. and midnight, residents asked to push their bikes, and police focusing on guidance at first.
sources.limits: A report of the first weekend (July 2026).

sources.title: The Hanoi Lake Where Kids Hustle American Tourists for English Lessons — The Wall Street Journal (republished by To Vima)
sources.org: The Wall Street Journal, by Stu Woo (republished by To Vima)
sources.used: Children sent by teachers and parents to approach tourists at the lake at weekends with clipboards of questions to practise English.
sources.limits: A feature of November 2026, read in a republished copy.

sources.title: Random conversations with foreigners won’t improve your English — VnExpress International
sources.org: VnExpress International (opinion), by Bui Minh Duc
sources.used: The habit of students approaching foreigners to practise English, and the writer’s view that it teaches little and can leave visitors uneasy.
sources.limits: An opinion piece (October 2023); readers replied with the opposite view.

sources.title: 130 năm chợ Đồng Xuân — Nhịp sống Hà Nội (Hà Nội Mới)
sources.org: Nhịp sống Hà Nội (Hà Nội Mới), by Thu Hằng
sources.used: The French merging the markets beside Cầu Đông pagoda and Bạch Mã temple at Đồng Xuân in 1889; its five arched entrances and five long halls; trams, the Long Biên bridge and the station making it the city’s “stomach”; the 1994 fire; three of the original gables kept in the rebuilding; more than 2,100 stalls; the night market since 2003.
sources.limits: An anniversary feature of October 2019, in Vietnamese.

sources.title: Chợ Đồng Xuân – Dấu ấn Hà Nội xưa giữa nhịp sống đương đại — Hà Nội Mới
sources.org: Hà Nội Mới (newspaper of the Hà Nội Party Committee), by Khánh Huy
sources.used: The market rebuilt after the 1994 fire on three floors of more than 14,000 m²; what each floor sells; hours of 6 a.m. to 6 p.m.; the weekend night market from 6 to 10.30 p.m.; its standing as one of the north’s largest wholesale markets.
sources.limits: A feature of November 2026, in Vietnamese. Another source gives closing time as 7 p.m.

sources.title: Ký ức chợ Hà Nội xưa — VnExpress
sources.used: Thăng Long once called Kẻ Chợ, “the market people”; Paul Bourde finding no covered market in 1883 and markets meeting every six days; Đồng Xuân formed from the Bạch Mã and Cầu Đông markets; market taxes under French rule; a seventeenth-century visitor noting street vendors beside the many markets.
sources.limits: A history feature of April 2022, in Vietnamese. It dates Đồng Xuân to 1890, where most sources give 1889.

sources.title: Eight landmark French-era buildings in downtown Hanoi — VnExpress International
sources.used: Đồng Xuân built in 1889, burnt in 1994 and rebuilt the following year for nearly 68 billion đồng with three storeys and more than 2,000 stores.
sources.limits: A travel feature of March 2021.

sources.title: Chợ Hà Nội – Tìm trong ký ức — Tuổi Trẻ Cuối tuần
sources.org: Tuổi Trẻ Cuối tuần, by Đỗ Phấn
sources.used: Đồng Xuân’s riveted steel trusses like those of the Long Biên bridge; only the front kept after the 1994 fire; in old village markets, sellers who believed a high opening price brought luck, and buyers who bargained to reach the right price rather than a cheap one.
sources.limits: A memoir-essay by a Hà Nội painter and writer (February 2015).

sources.title: Tấp nập khu chợ đêm mùa quả chín rẻ nhất Hà Nội — Tiền Phong
sources.used: Long Biên market founded in 1992 under the bridge, on more than 27,000 m²; goods laid out by about 11 p.m., busiest from midnight to 1 a.m., quiet by dawn; 200–300 tonnes of produce a day.
sources.limits: A news feature of July 2021.

sources.title: Những phụ nữ ở chợ đêm Long Biên — VnExpress
sources.used: Women porters at Long Biên, mostly in their thirties to fifties, carrying fruit loads of several hundred kilos from 3 a.m.
sources.limits: A feature of March 2009; pay figures in it are long out of date and not used.

sources.title: Vì sao nhiều người Hà Nội “nặng lòng” với chợ cóc? — VnExpress
sources.used: Chợ cóc on pavements, alleys and along railway lines; why people use them; a HealthBridge and Université de Montréal study finding about 100 chợ cóc against 25 official markets in four inner districts, serving nearly half the population within 300 m; renovated official markets losing buyers and sellers.
sources.limits: A feature of January 2026. Some figures it gives on traffic and food safety come from studies it does not name and are not used.

sources.title: Hà Nội đã sắp xếp được 98 “chợ cóc”, điểm kinh doanh tự phát — VnEconomy
sources.used: Hà Nội’s 468 markets by class; 231 chợ cóc and informal trading points identified and 98 dealt with; a timetable to June 2027; the city’s stance of firm but not extreme handling.
sources.limits: A report of January 2026. Other counts of the city’s markets differ by date.

sources.title: Food safety and urban food markets in Vietnam: The need for flexible and customized retail modernization policies — Food Policy 54: 95–106
sources.org: Food Policy (peer-reviewed), S. Wertheim-Heck, S. Vellema and G. Spaargaren
sources.used: The finding that replacing wet markets with supermarkets in Hà Nội reaches only a minor part of the population and pushes many shoppers towards informal vending.
sources.limits: Read as the published abstract and summary; research from the early 2010s.

sources.title: Văn hóa khai trương, mở hàng năm mới — VietNamNet
sources.used: The belief that the day’s first buyer brings luck and a failed first sale brings bad luck, so sellers avoid quoting the first customer too high; change given smoothly for the first sale; many such taboos fading.
sources.limits: A feature of February 2013 describing beliefs, not rules.

sources.title: Trải nghiệm ác mộng đi chợ ở Hà Nội: Bị hành hung, đốt vía, “quay xe” — Dân trí
sources.used: A Hà Nội seller pressing a shopper to buy because she had not yet made her first sale; hostility to shoppers who bargain and leave; the linguist Phạm Văn Tình’s view that the right to ask high and the right to bargain are equal.
sources.limits: A feature of December 2022 built on shoppers’ bad experiences, so not a picture of a typical market.

sources.title: Tourists overcharged? It’s a two-way street — VnExpress International
sources.org: VnExpress International (readers’ views), by Minh Minh
sources.used: Readers’ view that bargaining is expected in markets but haggling over tiny sums is unfair to vendors, and that malls have fixed prices for those who prefer not to bargain.
sources.limits: A round-up of reader comments (September 2023), so opinion.

sources.title: Overcharged in Vietnam: tips to avoid paying too much — VnExpress International
sources.used: Starting at about half to two-thirds of the asking price with vendors, raising slowly and staying polite; supermarkets for fixed prices.
sources.limits: A practical article of March 2016.

sources.title: What are the Vietnamese like? — vietnam.travel
sources.org: Vietnam National Authority of Tourism (official site)
sources.used: Lễ phép, politeness to elders; being asked your age at a first meeting; most homes having an ancestral altar; meals beginning when the oldest person takes the first bite; guests invited to stay for a meal and served by the host.
sources.limits: A general visitor page (2019) about Vietnam as a whole.

sources.title: How to meet and greet in Vietnamese — VnExpress International
sources.org: VnExpress International, by Pham Van and Kim Thuy
sources.used: Greeting with chào and a family word: cháu chào bác, cô, chú, ông or bà; adding ạ to show respect to elders; respect for elders as deeply rooted.
sources.limits: A short guide of August 2016. It says xin chào is rarely used in real conversation, where other guides treat it as standard.

sources.title: Nếp nhà Hà Nội — Znews (from “Chuyện người Hà Nội”)
sources.org: Znews, book excerpt by Vũ Thế Long (NXB Hà Nội and Tri thức Trẻ Books)
sources.used: In older Hà Nội families, friends who visited folded their arms to greet the parents and older siblings, and rude forms of address were strictly forbidden; the author describes these habits as fading.
sources.limits: A memoir of older Hà Nội family custom (published 2022), not a description of homes today.

sources.title: Eating and etiquette: Top tips for joining a VN family meal — VietNamNet
sources.org: VietNamNet (from Việt Nam News), by Eloise Levesque
sources.used: Not arriving empty-handed; fruit as the most popular gift, or something from your own country; hosts putting food in a guest’s bowl; leaving the last piece unless urged; being sent home with fruit.
sources.limits: A foreign contributor’s first-hand account (October 2013).

sources.title: Những món quà “kiêng” tặng ngày tết — VietNamNet
sources.used: Folk beliefs about gifts to avoid at Tết: knives and scissors, clocks, dark wrapping, and others, some of them regional.
sources.limits: A Tết feature of January 2013 describing beliefs, not rules.

sources.title: Vị thế của trà — Sài Gòn Giải Phóng
sources.org: Sài Gòn Giải Phóng (newspaper), by Nguyễn Ngọc Tuấn
sources.used: Hosts brewing a fresh pot when guests arrive; the saying that a cup of tea starts the conversation; not offering tea seen as impolite.
sources.limits: An essay of February 2021 on tea across Vietnam, not only Hà Nội.

sources.title: Ý nghĩa thiêng liêng của bàn thờ gia tiên trong gia đình người Việt — VietnamPlus
sources.used: The ancestral altar as the most sacred place in the home, at its centre and highest point; the flowers offered on it at Tết, chrysanthemums among them.
sources.limits: A Tết feature of January 2023.

sources.title: Bàn thờ tổ tiên – đôi điều nhân nghĩa — Dân trí
sources.used: Altars in the middle of traditional houses and often on the top floor today; the old custom of placing a visitor’s gift on the altar, now largely gone; northern and southern customs differing.
sources.limits: An opinion piece of February 2021.

sources.title: Ancestor worship reminds people of their roots — VietNamNet
sources.used: Altars in homes rich and poor, in a prominent place, with tablets and photographs, an incense bowl and candles.
sources.limits: A feature of January 2020.

sources.title: Văn hóa “mời cơm” đang biến mất? — VnExpress
sources.used: The northern custom of younger family members inviting their elders, in order, to eat before picking up their chopsticks; its fading as families share fewer meals; a 2021 Nielsen figure of about 45% of families eating dinner together five times a week or more.
sources.limits: A feature of August 2025. The invitation it describes is between family members, not from host to guest.

sources.title: Nên hay không gắp đồ ăn cho người khác? — Báo Thế giới & Việt Nam
sources.org: Báo Thế giới & Việt Nam (newspaper of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs), protocol column
sources.used: Hosts placing food in guests’ bowls as affection; the column’s advice that with less familiar guests, especially foreigners, hosts should invite in words only and not press food on them; a guest’s polite reply, let me help myself.
sources.limits: A protocol column of December 2019 arguing for a modern view.

sources.title: “Ăn cơm chưa, đi đâu đấy?” — VnExpress
sources.org: VnExpress (opinion), by Đinh Võ Kiều Oanh
sources.used: “Have you eaten yet?” as a greeting and often an invitation to stay and eat; the proverb that a greeting is worth more than a feast.
sources.limits: An opinion piece of January 2025.

sources.title: Press release: preliminary results of the 2019 Population and Housing Census
sources.used: An average of 3.5 people per household nationally, 3.3 in cities and in the Red River Delta, the region that includes Hà Nội.
sources.limits: Preliminary figures (2019); no figure for Hà Nội alone and no data on generations.

sources.title: The generation of elderly who do not live with their children — VietNamNet
sources.used: Two studies that disagree: one finding the share of older people living with their children fell from about 80% in 1992–93 to 28% in 2017 in two provinces, another national survey finding more than 60% still do.
sources.limits: A feature of February 2022 that does not reconcile the two figures.

sources.title: 4 câu người EQ cao không bao giờ nói khi đến thăm nhà người khác — Báo Văn Hóa
sources.org: Báo Văn Hóa, by Tathiên An
sources.used: Choosing a natural pause to leave and thanking the host sincerely for their hospitality; not looking at the clock or saying you are tired.
sources.limits: A general lifestyle piece (December 2025).

sources.title: Xe điện dần thay đổi thói quen đi lại của người dân Hà Nội — Đại biểu Nhân dân
sources.org: Đại biểu Nhân dân (newspaper of the National Assembly), by Thanh Bình
sources.used: About 6.9 million motorbikes and 1.1 million cars in Hà Nội, and more than 450,000 motorbikes inside Ring Road 1.
sources.limits: A report of May 2026; the citywide totals may repeat 2025 figures.

sources.title: Thủ tướng yêu cầu Hà Nội thực hiện lộ trình đến ngày 1.7.2026 không có xe máy sử dụng nhiên liệu hóa thạch lưu thông trong Vành đai 1 — Báo Văn Hóa
sources.org: Báo Văn Hóa, by Tùng Quang
sources.used: Directive 20/CT-TTg of 12 July 2025, asking Hà Nội to have no petrol motorbikes inside Ring Road 1 from 1 July 2026, with wider limits in 2028 and 2030.
sources.limits: A newspaper’s report of the directive (July 2025); we could not open the directive itself.

sources.title: Hanoi drops proposal for outright petrol motorbike ban around Hoan Kiem Lake — VietNamNet
sources.used: The city dropping an outright ban on petrol motorbikes in the centre in favour of phases: a small zone around the lake and Old Quarter in 2026, two wards in 2027, the whole of Ring Road 1 in 2028–2029.
sources.limits: A report of May 2026, before the final vote.

sources.title: Xử lý hơn 3,3 triệu trường hợp vi phạm giao thông trong năm 2025 — Báo Văn Hóa
sources.org: Báo Văn Hóa (citing the National Traffic Safety Committee)
sources.used: 10,379 road deaths nationally between mid-December 2024 and mid-December 2025, down about 6% on the year before.
sources.limits: Police-recorded figures (January 2026), which count fewer deaths than WHO’s modelled estimates.

sources.title: 9 tháng năm 2026, toàn quốc xảy ra 11.564 vụ tai nạn giao thông — VietnamPlus
sources.used: 7,198 traffic deaths nationally in the first nine months of 2026, down 9% on a year earlier.
sources.limits: Police-recorded figures (October 2026).

sources.title: Việt Nam’s road accident-related deaths fall by 43.5 per cent in 2011-20 — Việt Nam News
sources.org: Việt Nam News (citing the WHO Global Status Report on Road Safety 2023)
sources.used: WHO’s estimated road death rate for Vietnam falling from 25.4 per 100,000 people in 2010 to 17.7 in 2021.
sources.limits: A news report (December 2023) of WHO’s modelled estimates, which are not comparable with police counts.

sources.title: Đi bộ qua đường không có tín hiệu bằng tay phạt đến 250.000 đồng — LuatVietnam
sources.used: Decree 168/2024 Article 10(1): fines of 150,000–250,000 đồng for pedestrians who walk in the wrong part of the road, climb medians, cross in the wrong place, cross without a hand signal where one is required, or ignore lights or police; 60,000–100,000 đồng before 2025.
sources.limits: A legal news summary (January 2025).

sources.title: Vẫy tay thế nào cho đúng khi đi bộ qua đường? — Znews
sources.used: That no hand signal is needed on a marked crossing, and that the decree does not say how the hand signal should be made.
sources.limits: An explainer of January 2025.

sources.title: Đi bộ qua đường, chịu khó bước lại vạch trắng và vẫy tay — Tuổi Trẻ
sources.used: Raising a hand described as a long-standing good habit, and the writers’ view that drivers yield more since Decree 168.
sources.limits: An opinion piece (February 2025).

sources.title: “Vạch kẻ đường vô hình” — VnExpress
sources.used: A reader counting 37 people crossing during one red light at a Hà Nội junction, only 4 of them on the zebra crossing; blocked pavements and short green lights; a motorbike-taxi driver’s advice to walk evenly, look ahead and not stop, run or hesitate.
sources.limits: A reader’s opinion piece (May 2026), not a study.

sources.title: Three seconds of morality — Việt Nam News
sources.org: Việt Nam News (“Talk Around Town” column), by Bảo Long
sources.used: The columnist’s view that vehicles in Hà Nội rarely stop for pedestrians; walking steadily and keeping eye contact while riders adjust just enough to pass.
sources.limits: A newspaper column (December 2025), so opinion.

sources.title: Civil Code No. 91/2015/QH13, Articles 32 and 38 (unofficial English translation)
sources.org: National Assembly of Vietnam (translation hosted by economica.vn)
sources.used: Article 32: a person’s rights over their image, consent needed to use it, payment for commercial use, the exceptions for public interest and public events, and court remedies; Article 38 on private life.
sources.limits: An unofficial translation “for reference only”. The article governs using an image, such as publishing it, not taking it.

sources.title: Decree 218/2025/NĐ-CP on penalties for administrative violations in national defence (Chapter 2, Sections 7 and 9)
sources.used: Fines of 20–30 million đồng and confiscation for filming or photographing in the restricted and protected zones of the Hồ Chí Minh Mausoleum site; 5–8 million đồng for photographing in a military prohibited area, and 30–50 million in special-category zones.
sources.limits: Read on a third-party legal database (Sections 7 and 9).

sources.short: Tạp chí Tòa án nhân dân
sources.title: Họp báo công bố Pháp lệnh Quản lý, bảo vệ khu di tích lăng Chủ tịch Hồ Chí Minh — Tạp chí Tòa án nhân dân
sources.org: Tạp chí Tòa án nhân dân (journal of the People’s Courts)
sources.used: The ordinance on managing and protecting the Mausoleum relic site, adopted on 13 March 2025 and in force from 19 May 2025.
sources.limits: A report of the press conference (April 2025).

sources.title: Ban hành quy định quản lý tàu bay không người lái và phương tiện bay khác — VnEconomy
sources.used: Decree 288/2025 on drones, in force from 5 November 2025, requiring a licence to fly aircraft of 0.25 kg and over.
sources.limits: A news summary (November 2025); we did not confirm which older rules it replaces.

sources.title: Illegal drone flights face fines of up to VND 40 million — DTiNews
sources.used: Fines under Decree 282/2025 from 15 December 2025: 8–9 million đồng for aerial photos or video without permission, 2–3 million for flying without registration or a permit, up to 40 million for endangering aviation; Hà Nội police warning against flights near military and restricted sites.
sources.limits: A news report (June 2026).

sources.title: Visiting regulations — Imperial Citadel of Thang Long
sources.org: Thăng Long – Hà Nội Heritage Conservation Centre (hoangthanhthanglong.vn)
sources.used: Prior permission needed to make films or visual recordings at the site; no drones; neat, polite dress.
sources.limits: Rules dated 2013; nothing on ordinary still photos.

sources.title: Những việc nên và không nên làm khi ghé thăm một ngôi chùa Phật giáo — VOV
sources.org: Voice of Vietnam (VOV), by Hà Phương (adapted from Business Insider)
sources.used: Temples as places of worship; no flash where signs ask for no photos; photographing the Buddha often seen as disrespectful, and selfies with statues as controversial.
sources.limits: A general guide to Buddhist temples (December 2015), adapted from an English article.

sources.title: Hanoi punishes street vendors for harassing foreigners — DTiNews
sources.used: Hoàn Kiếm district acting against nearly 140 vendors in 2012 who put their shoulder poles on tourists for photos and then demanded money, many of them repeat offenders.
sources.limits: A report from 2012; we found no recent figures, so this is described as a long-reported practice.

sources.title: Vietnamese culture: Core Concepts — The Cultural Atlas
sources.org: The Cultural Atlas (Mosaica), Cultural Atlas Editors
sources.used: Face as reputation, influence, dignity and honour; giving face through respect and compliments and losing it through criticism; indirect, polite speech; modesty (khiêm tốn) as keeping harmony; the note that modesty does not preclude honesty and that views vary by region, age and education.
sources.limits: A general guide (2016) for Vietnam as a whole.

sources.title: Vietnamese culture: Communication — The Cultural Atlas
sources.org: The Cultural Atlas (Mosaica), Cultural Atlas Editors
sources.used: Indirect communication; avoiding a flat no; a yes that may mean “I hear you”; pausing before answering as politeness; shouting seen as improper yet common; smiling when embarrassed or nervous; sombre expressions that are not unfriendly; pointing and beckoning with an open hand; the head as sacred; feet, hands on hips and the “okay” sign.
sources.limits: A general guide (2016); it describes tendencies, not rules.

sources.title: How Do the Vietnamese Lose Face? Understanding the Concept of Face through Self-Reported, Face Loss Incidents — International Journal of Language and Linguistics 2(3): 223–231
sources.org: International Journal of Language and Linguistics, Pham Thi Hong Nhung (Hue University of Foreign Languages)
sources.used: The finding that Vietnamese face (mất mặt, mất thể diện) is both an individual and a collective possession and depends on how others judge.
sources.limits: Read as the published abstract only.

sources.title: “Thể diện linh thiêng”: Cái gì định hướng người Việt Nam trong tương tác xã hội thường nhật — Vietnam Journal of Social Sciences and Humanities
sources.org: VNU University of Social Sciences and Humanities, Nguyễn Trung Kiên
sources.used: The distinction between the face of people higher and lower in a hierarchy, and the finding that loss of face by someone higher up has more serious consequences.
sources.limits: Read as the published abstract only (2015).

sources.title: Nghiên cứu trở lại vấn đề thể diện và lịch sự trong giao tiếp — VNU Journal of Foreign Studies
sources.org: VNU Journal of Foreign Studies (University of Languages and International Studies, Hà Nội), Nguyễn Quang
sources.used: A Vietnamese host’s mock scolding of a guest for bringing a gift, comfortable for a Vietnamese guest but not for an American one; the author’s warning that such observations are hypotheses, not stereotypes.
sources.limits: A theoretical paper (2019) by a Hà Nội linguist.

sources.title: Nghiên cứu về danh dự gia đình ở Việt Nam: Vấn đề khái niệm và hướng tiếp cận — Thông tin Khoa học xã hội
sources.org: Social Sciences Information Review no. 5 (2022), Nguyễn Thanh Tùng
sources.used: Danh dự, thể diện, sĩ diện and related words being used almost interchangeably; thể diện as the social form of honour, extended to the group; older critiques of “sĩ diện hão”, hollow vanity.
sources.limits: A review of concepts (2022) that itself calls for caution.

sources.title: Vietnamese culture: Naming — The Cultural Atlas
sources.org: The Cultural Atlas (Mosaica), by Nina Evason
sources.used: Kinship titles used for non-relatives, chosen by age, gender, status and region; anh, chị, chú, cô, bác, ông, bà and em by relative age; cháu for a much younger person in the North and con in the Centre and South; bạn mainly among young people of the same age; the title placed before the given name.
sources.limits: A general guide (2025) for Vietnam as a whole.

sources.title: Chủ quan tính và khách quan tính trong hệ thống xưng hô Việt và Anh — VNU Journal of Foreign Studies 34(1): 16–34
sources.org: VNU Journal of Foreign Studies (University of Languages and International Studies, Hà Nội), Nguyễn Quang
sources.used: Speakers classifying themselves and others by kinship, position and age; the northern pairing cháu–bác or cháu–chú, used in both directions; respect when both halves of a pair are used and intimacy when one is dropped; a 1992 survey in which 428 of 562 responses used kinship terms; northern speakers using chú and cô rather than dì or cậu for strangers of their parents’ age; tôi as formal and distant, and once meaning a king’s subject.
sources.limits: An academic paper (2018) whose author calls his findings preliminary remarks, not stereotypes.

sources.title: Vietnamese terms of address: Pragmatic connotations, translation and ESL/EFL pedagogy — PhD thesis, University of New England
sources.org: University of New England (Australia), Ton Nu Linh Thoai
sources.used: Address terms whose feeling depends on context; tôi as the only fairly neutral pronoun, formal in everyday use; tớ–cậu as a casual northern pair; learners over-using tôi and bạn, which sounds unnatural between middle-aged neighbours; a study of 500 market conversations in four cities in which 80% of questions used kinship forms.
sources.limits: A doctoral thesis (2017) written partly from a Central and Southern perspective.

sources.title: Basic Vietnamese, Unit 1 and Unit 6 culture notes — Michigan State University open textbook
sources.org: Michigan State University Libraries, by Tung Hoang
sources.used: Family terms and what they cover: bác for a parent’s older sibling, chú for a father’s younger brother, cô for a father’s younger sister, cậu for a mother’s younger brother, dì for a mother’s younger sister; the note that rules differ by region.
sources.limits: An open textbook (2023, CC BY-NC 4.0) for beginners.

sources.title: Thú vị sự khác biệt của gia đình Việt các vùng miền — Báo Pháp luật Việt Nam
sources.org: Báo Pháp luật Việt Nam, by Ngọc Mai
sources.used: Northern bố and mẹ against southern ba and má; the eldest brother called anh cả in the North and anh hai in the South, where anh hai in the North is the second brother.
sources.limits: A light feature (July 2016).

sources.title: Sơ đồ cách xưng hô trong họ hàng — VOH
sources.org: Voice of Hồ Chí Minh City (VOH), by Hồng Phượng
sources.used: Great-grandparents called cụ in the North and cố in the South; folding your arms and nodding when unsure how to address an older person.
sources.limits: A practical explainer (January 2025).
